title: SRM-LoRA: Steering LoRA's Gradients Away from Hallucination-Prone Directions
hook: Most LoRA variants just shrink how many parameters you tune. SRM-LoRA changes which directions get updated at all — using geometry to steer fine-tuning away from directions tied to hallucination.
key_points: SRM-LoRA builds a sensitivity-based Riemannian metric over the LoRA parameter space, inspired by sub-Riemannian geometry.
That metric reshapes backward gradients during fine-tuning, suppressing updates along 'high-cost' directions associated with hallucination.
Forward computation and inference cost are left unchanged — the intervention is purely in how gradients update the adapter during training.
Accepted at the ICML 2026 workshop FoGen, with an official implementation released on GitHub.
content_html: Most parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods focus on cutting how many weights you touch. A new method called SRM-LoRA instead targets which directions in that reduced parameter space get updated, using a geometry-inspired metric to specifically dial down directions linked to hallucination.
extra_html: A Reddit user shared their research, accepted at the ICML 2026 FoGen workshop: SRM-LoRA builds a sensitivity-based Riemannian metric over LoRA's parameter space and uses it to reshape backward gradients during fine-tuning, suppressing updates along "high-cost" directions the authors tie to hallucination. The forward pass and inference cost are left untouched — the change is purely in how the adapter's own weights get updated during training. An official implementation is linked on GitHub via the source post.

related.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
related.hook: Why retrain billions of weights when you can freeze them all and train tiny add-on matrices instead? LoRA tunes under ~1% of the parameters with near-full-fine-tune quality.

related.title: QLoRA: Fine-tuning Quantized LLMs
related.hook: Fine-tune a model with tens of billions of parameters on a single GPU. QLoRA squeezes the frozen base to 4-bit, then trains LoRA adapters on top — without losing quality.
